nameStory: The blood ark clam gets its dramatic name from its unusual red blood, which contains hemoglobin just like ours! Most clams and other mollusks have clear or bluish blood, making this little shellfish a true standout. The 'ark' part of its name comes from its boat-like shell shape, resembling the biblical ark.
description: The blood ark is a small clam that lives in shallow waters along New England's coast. These clams typically measure 1-3 inches long and have distinctively boat-shaped shells. What makes them really stand out is their dark brown, fur-like covering called periostracum that can cover up to two-thirds of their shell, giving them a fuzzy, almost mammal-like appearance. Unlike most clams, they have bright red blood that's visible when the shell is opened.

idTips.label: Fuzzy brown covering
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive dark brown, fur-like coating that covers most of the shell - it feels rough and fibrous to the touch, almost like a wet animal pelt

idTips.label: Boat-shaped shell
idTips.description: The shell has an elongated, ark-like shape that's wider at one end, unlike the round or oval shells of most other clams

idTips.label: Size range
idTips.description: Typically 1-3 inches in length, fitting comfortably in your palm - smaller than quahogs but larger than many beach pebbles

idTips.label: Red blood
idTips.description: If you find a fresh specimen, the blood inside is distinctly red rather than clear - though you'll need to open the shell to see this

idTips.label: Shell texture beneath
idTips.description: Where the fuzzy covering has worn away, the shell underneath appears white to grayish with distinct growth lines you can feel with your fingertip

habitat: Blood arks live in shallow coastal waters from the low-tide line down to about 10 feet deep. You'll find their shells washed up on sandy and muddy beaches throughout New England, especially after storms. They prefer areas with some protection from heavy surf, often in bays, estuaries, and calmer coastal waters where they can burrow into soft sediments.

seasonality.spring: Fresh shells may wash ashore after spring storms, when the fuzzy brown covering is most intact and easiest to identify.
seasonality.summer: Peak beachcombing season for finding blood ark shells, as calm weather makes beach exploration ideal and the shells are often well-preserved.
seasonality.fall: Autumn storms frequently wash shells onto beaches, though the fuzzy covering may be more worn by this time of year.
seasonality.winter: Winter storms can bring shells ashore, but cold weather and harsh conditions mean fewer people are out looking for them.

funFact: Blood ark clams are one of the very few animals besides vertebrates that have red blood with hemoglobin - the same oxygen-carrying protein that makes our blood red! This makes them incredibly unusual in the mollusk world, where most relatives have blue or clear blood instead.
confusionNotes: The fuzzy brown covering makes blood arks pretty distinctive, but worn shells without the periostracum might be confused with other small clams. Remember the boat-shaped shell and look for any remaining patches of that characteristic dark brown fuzz - even small remnants are a dead giveaway.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'Lunarca' refers to the moon-like curved shape of the shell. While called 'blood ark clams,' they're actually in the ark clam family (Arcidae), which gets its name from the boat or ark-like shape shared by many species in this group.
compareHints: Since blood arks are the only Lunarca species in New England waters, compare them to other ark clams in the family Arcidae. Blood arks are generally smaller and have more extensive fuzzy covering than most other ark clams. Their boat-like shape is less pronounced than some ark clam relatives, and that distinctive dark brown periostracum covering two-thirds of the shell is uniquely theirs.
